html:
GPU telemetry and configuration

Enable GPU in Capabilities to inspect and configure devices on the selected Gateway. The skill starts disabled. Discovery grants no execution or OS privilege. The Gateway advertises gpu_telemetry and gpu_configuration when nvidia-smi is installed; every operation checks current driver and device support. These tags do not promise that every setting is supported. There is no controller fallback, automatic installation, arbitrary argv tool or helper inference.

Discover gpu for gpu.status, gpu.devices, gpu.device, gpu.processes and gpu.sample. Further tools are grouped as follows:

Section Tools
gpu.telemetry status, devices, device, sample
gpu.processes processes
gpu.configuration power_limits, set_power_limit, restore_power_limit, set_persistence_mode, set_compute_mode, clock_capabilities, set_gpu_clock_range, reset_gpu_clocks, set_memory_clock_range, reset_memory_clocks
gpu.advanced reset_status, reset

All tool IDs use the gpu. prefix. Advanced tools are absent from entry discovery. Reads have the read effect. Configuration has the broad write effect and retains the existing gpu_configuration classification and exact resource descriptors in execution receipts.

Console data and lifecycle flows trace the independent diagnostic sidecar, its cached observations, local GPU readings and explicit stack capture. Diagnostic findings do not establish task completion.

Implementation ownership

flowchart LR Tool[Authorized typed GPU tool] --> Controller[Controller GPU service] Controller --> Transport[Selected-Gateway client] Transport --> Gateway[Node-bound GPU service] Gateway --> Reads[Bounded observations and sampling] Gateway --> Admission[UUID job admission and Local AI coordination] Admission --> Provider[NVIDIA argv adapter] Reads --> Provider Provider --> Readback[Fresh UUID readback] Readback --> Receipt[Verified state or explicit uncertainty]
Owner Responsibility
Skill definitions and tools Discovery sections, hard argument validation, effects, resource class, confirmation and cancellation transport.
Controller service One requested dispatch and a separate observation when a mutation's outcome is unknown.
Gateway client Authenticated selected-node envelope, response bounds and independent cancellation.
Gateway service Call admission, recent IDs, sampling, job/resource ownership and configuration readback.
Provider interface and NVIDIA adapter Typed operations, strict argv grammar, bounded helper lifetime and current hardware observations.
Shared contracts and telemetry parser Closed inputs, private reset authority, canonical errors and consistent null/unit conversion.

Identity and telemetry

The NVIDIA UUID is durable mutation authority. device accepts a UUID or a current display index. An index mutation also requires expected_uuid from discovery, binding approval to that device. The Gateway resolves the index before admission and checks again after acquiring ownership; all subprocess mutations use --id GPU-…. Device reorder never redirects a mutation.

Inventory includes UUID, index, name, utilization, used/total VRAM bytes, VRAM percentage, temperature in Celsius, power draw and current power limit in watts. Detail adds PCI bus ID, driver version, architecture, current/default/minimum/maximum power, persistence, compute mode, MIG/ECC state and clock observations. Compute capability remains null in this initial adapter. Unsupported or non-finite metrics are null. Clock observations are instantaneous frequencies, not proof of configured constraints. Console telemetry, server utilization and GPU tools share numeric/CSV parsing in gateway_core/gpu/telemetry.py.

processes reads NVIDIA's XML compute/graphics process list. It returns up to 1,024 PIDs, process basenames, process types, GPU UUIDs and available memory values, with observation time and available provider timestamps. An unavailable or truncated process list is explicitly incomplete and cannot authorize reset. There is no OS PID join, inferred ownership, argument or environment capture, process kill, or background process watcher. Exact task results retain needed metadata; diagnostic and portable-history projections omit process content.

Bounded sampling

Supply interval_seconds and exactly one of samples or duration_seconds, with optional UUIDs and fields. Intervals are 0.5–60 seconds; at most 120 samples spanning at most 300 seconds are accepted. Duration includes an initial sample at time zero. For example, five-second samples for one minute produce 13 observations. Requests outside these bounds fail explicitly. Selection is pinned to the first observation's UUIDs when omitted. Disappearance fails with identity-change evidence rather than substituting a device at the same index.

One Gateway call performs the whole sample, using cancellation-aware waits. There are at most 16 active calls per service, 64 devices per inventory, 2 MiB per provider response and 8 MiB per transport response. Each NVIDIA child has a five-second deadline; configuration/read requests have a 45-second budget and sampling a 330-second budget. Long or conditional watches belong to the existing Monitor skill. Sampling never causes one Agent turn per interval.

The controller transport allows 60 seconds for ordinary calls and 340 seconds for sampling. Cancellation uses /gpu/cancel independently of the pending observation. Its acknowledgement confirms that the service signalled/remembered the execution ID; it does not prove a hardware change was undone. The service rejects active or recent execution IDs, retaining at most 4,096 recent IDs for ten minutes in RAM. Mutation job identity is a separate retained-state check described below.

Configuration and privileges

The adapter uses argv with shell=False; the existing nvidia_smi_effect grammar validates both queries and compiled mutations. Current Shell grammar, wrappers and unsafe behavior remain unchanged. The installed CLI help and fresh per-device queries gate configuration. The driver can still reject an otherwise eligible operation; the result reports that rejection.

Power changes query and validate finite hardware min/max/default/current values before mutation and again after admission. Values are never clamped. Restore uses the queried default, with no model-specific table. The exact requested value is checked against fresh readback. Persistence uses explicit booleans and is Linux-only. Compute mode accepts default, prohibited or exclusive_process (documented CLI values 0, 2 and 3), then reads the resulting state.

Clock setters accept integer minimum/maximum MHz endpoints found in the current device's supported clock pairs. Unsupported endpoints and reversed ranges fail before mutation. GPU clock locks are restricted to recognized Volta-or-later architectures with queried supported clocks and installed CLI flags. Memory locks also exclude Hopper's deferred mechanism. Deprecated application clocks, deferred memory locks, voltage changes and fan control are not exposed.

NVIDIA's CLI does not provide a reliable query of locked-clock constraints. An acknowledged clock command returns verified: false, current clock telemetry, and verification: provider_acknowledged_constraints_unobservable. It never labels current frequency as a verified lock. Lost clock acknowledgements remain unknown.

Configuration uses ordinary Permission policy. GPU reset also uses the existing Unsafe Action policy, bound to the exact request. The Gateway receives that authority through the trusted runtime envelope, never model arguments. If the OS account lacks permission, the skill returns gpu.permission_denied with operator remediation. It never invents sudo or retains root passwords.

Reset and provider limits

Provider / operation Initial support
NVIDIA telemetry / process metadata Queried per device; null/incomplete when unavailable
NVIDIA power / persistence / compute Fresh queries, installed CLI and driver acceptance; OS privilege required
NVIDIA GPU/memory clocks Queried endpoints and documented architecture restrictions; no constraint readback claim
NVIDIA reset Linux, one physical GPU, inactive display, MIG disabled/unsupported, complete empty client list, current unsafe authority
Multi-GPU peer / NVSwitch reset Refused; peer/Fabric Manager reset orchestration is not modeled
MIG / ECC configuration Not exposed; available state is telemetry only
AMD / Apple No adapter; no emulated parity

Reset checks current clients after acquiring resource ownership. Any active client blocks reset; unknown clients, active displays, virtualization, MIG, or unproven peer scope fail closed. It never kills clients. Successful reset re-discovers the UUID and reports query/readback health; this is not a hardware diagnostic certification. A lost reset response causes one probe and an unknown-outcome receipt, even if the device is visible. Reset is never automatically repeated.

Resources and unknown outcomes

Gateway configuration registers a job using the existing GatewayJobs admission authority, claiming gpu:<gateway>:<uuid>. Same-device configuration serializes. Reads carry lightweight capacity and do not acquire mutation claims, so GPU B reads remain possible while GPU A changes. Native configuration uses gpu_heavy capacity; the configured per-Gateway limit still applies. Opaque Shell/model jobs conservatively overlap through existing wildcard ownership.

When the applicable GPU resource-locking policy is enabled, Local AI start and GPU configuration share a short admission lock and a count of active configuration owners; disjoint GPU changes can proceed concurrently. Configuration fails promptly if startup owns the lock or an owned runtime remains live/unknown. This initial local-AI policy blocks configuration conservatively across all GPUs. Unresolved GPU configuration also fences new local-AI starts until resource ownership is reconciled. Ordinary external workloads may coexist with power, persistence, compute and clock changes, subject to NVIDIA's own rejection. Reset always requires an empty complete client list. Unrelated external applications are not controlled by SMTO's scheduler, so the driver's final client check remains necessary.

Blocked operations return gpu.resource_busy with the Gateway job ID, available blocking job IDs and the existing correlated resource facts/revision. There is no indefinite admission wait. A retained gpu_<execution_id> job rejects reuse of that mutation identity. This is separate from the short recent-ID cache. The current Gateway state owner publishes RAM transactions and saves background recovery generations; registration and updates are not individual synchronous disk barriers. Crash recovery can restore only saved state and independent retained evidence. See Gateway state and recovery for that boundary; the GPU adapter does not establish exactly-once hardware execution across arbitrary crashes.

The GPU job records a reconciliation requirement before dispatch: generic abandoned-job repair cannot clear a hardware outcome merely because its command ended. Explicit existing job recovery remains available after inspecting current device state; resetting a job claim does not reset hardware.

Lost response Reconciliation
Power set / restore Query current value (and current default for restore); report success only if desired state is observed
Persistence / compute Query exact state and compare
Clock set / reset Query telemetry, retain gpu.operation_outcome_unknown; constraints are not observable
Device reset Probe UUID/device; retain unknown and never issue a second reset
Re-probe unavailable Retain unknown and resource reconciliation requirement

Each dispatch boundary sends the mutation once. After a possibly applied command, the Gateway makes a fresh readback attempt with a twelve-second budget, even after request cancellation or timeout. If the controller loses that receipt or receives an unknown outcome, it may make its own separate device read with a new execution ID. Neither path reapplies the mutation. A helper that might still be executing prevents successful reconciliation even when a value happens to match. Readback proves current desired state; it cannot prove which concurrent actor caused that state.

Errors and validation

GPU errors are canonical gpu.* aliases in the Error Catalog (SMTO-GWT-0058 through SMTO-GWT-0082). They cover provider/driver absence, identity change, unsupported metrics/configuration, privileges, power/clock ranges, active clients, reset restrictions, resource contention, sample bounds, cancellation/timeouts, unknown outcomes, invalid requests/responses, connection loss, duplicates and unsafe confirmation. Provider stderr and process arguments are never copied into errors.

Deterministic tests inject fake NVIDIA argv responses and use real Gateway job admission. They cover UUID reorder, null metrics, old/new XML power layouts, processes, typed configuration, readback, permission errors, clock restrictions, reset refusal/success/lost response, sampling cancellation, resource contention, authenticated inbound/outbound routing, policy/discovery, privacy and zero helpers.

Optional live smoke is strictly read-only:

SMTO_GPU_SMOKE=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_gpu_live.py

The smoke replaces the mutation entry point with a test failure and asserts every subprocess is classified read-only. No configuration smoke is supplied or run; real changes need a separate explicit operator procedure with prior-state restoration.

The original implementation recorded checks against NVIDIA-SMI 580.159.03; that is historical validation, not a claim about the current host's installed driver. The implementation report retains its original results. The documentation review checks current source and deterministic fixtures without running the optional live smoke. NVIDIA maintains its CLI reference.
